question: After years of unjustified delays, in December 2023 the Council took the unanimous decision to welcome Romania and Bulgaria into the Schengen area, starting with the lifting of controls at air and sea borders only, as of March 2024. The decision on lifting controls at land borders is still pending.

Against this backdrop, a widely debated idea has emerged, proposing the rapid creation of a miniSchengen zone between Greece, Romania and Bulgaria, to be operational by the summer of 2024, in order to ease the heavy border traffic between the three countries. In this context: 1.

What is the Commission’s assessment of the concept of creating a mini-Schengen zone to lift controls at the land borders between Bulgaria, Romania and Greece until a final decision in this regard has been taken by the Council?
Does the Commission consider the concept technically and logistically possible and feasible?
Would the Commission consider such action to be compatible with the Schengen acquis and EU law?
answer: Protocol No 19 on the Schengen acquis integrated into the framework of the EU (1) underlines the need to preserve the integrity of the Schengen acquis. It lists a limited number of possible derogations to that principle, such as the deferred application of parts of the Schengen acquis in new Member States.

Both Article 4 of the 2005 Act of Accession of Bulgaria and Romania (2) and Council Decision (EU) 2024/210 on the full application of the provisions of the Schengen acquis in Bulgaria and Romania (3) aim at paving the way to a full application of the Schengen acquis in these two Member States.

Protocol No 19 defines Schengen as a ‘closer cooperation between some Member States’ to which the rules on enhanced cooperation, set out in Articles 326 to 334 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, apply. These rules do not allow any other form of enhanced cooperation within an already existing enhanced cooperation.
The adoption of Council Decision (EU) 2024/210 meant that as of 31 March 2024, the controls at Romania and Bulgaria’s air and sea borders have been lifted.

The Council also agreed a further decision should be taken for the lifting of checks at internal land borders, which are currently maintained between the land borders of Romania and Bulgaria and other Schengen Member States as well as between Romania and Bulgaria.

As regards border checks at the only remaining element, the internal land borders, all efforts are now being taken to allow the Council to lift these checks as soon as possible. The Commission actively supports this process and hopes that the Council will take such decision soon.
